analysis.one_liner: Bars leasing of federal land with little or no oil and gas potential, ending speculative leasing.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote; it died in the House Natural Resources Committee after being referred there in May 2021 and to two subcommittees in June 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the government to actually assess whether a parcel of federal land can produce oil or gas before offering it for lease, and to stop leasing parcels designated as having low or no potential. It carries exceptions so leasing near producing wells can continue, and it allows companies to seek a variance with public review if they can show a lease would serve the public interest. The aim is to stop companies from cheaply locking up public land that will likely never produce oil or gas, which ties up the land for other uses and yields almost no revenue for taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently get minimal revenue from leases on land with little or no oil potential and pay for the government to issue and manage those leases [S3]. Also people who use public land for grazing, recreation, wildlife, and other purposes, since speculative leases can block those uses [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Before offering land for lease, the Bureau of Land Management would have to complete or update an assessment of each parcel's oil and gas potential, and could not lease land designated as having low or no potential except in narrow cases.

The bill's findings state that no- or low-potential land is often leased at or near the minimum bid or noncompetitively, rarely produces oil or gas, and yields taxpayers minimal revenue while costing the government resources to administer.
Leasing near producing wells — for drainage prevention or small parcels within a mile of a producing well — would still be allowed, so ongoing production would not be disrupted.

Companies could still obtain a variance to lease low- or no-potential land by proving in a public process that the lease would not harm wildlife, recreation, water, air, or protected areas, and is in the public interest, with a limit of one variance per applicant every five years.

The bill would add public notice and comment periods of at least 60 days for the assessments and for variance applications, giving the public a say in leasing decisions the findings say currently lack meaningful participation.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies and speculators, who would lose the ability to cheaply acquire leases on federal land with little or no production potential, and would face a longer, more public process before leasing land of uncertain potential. The government would also bear the cost of conducting and regularly updating the assessments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas lessees and speculators

drawbacks.text: Requiring assessments and 15-year updates, with 60-day public comment periods, before any lease sale would add time and administrative cost to the federal leasing program, including for parcels of uncertain potential that might turn out to be productive.

Critics of limiting federal leasing argue it could reduce future domestic oil and gas supply, though the bill states its policies are not detrimental to U.S. energy security and preserves leasing near producing wells.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted rather than sweeping: it stops the cheapest form of speculative leasing — locking up land the government's own analysis says will not produce — while leaving normal leasing near producing wells untouched and providing a variance path for unusual cases. The costs are real but modest: slower leasing paperwork for the government and lost cheap lease opportunities for companies. An honest supporter would acknowledge the added process could delay some legitimate leasing.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its subcommittees for the rest of the Congress and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Susie Lee introduced the bill on May 4, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
Five Democratic cosponsors signed on; no Republicans did.
On June 19, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources and the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023; the bill was never marked up, never left committee, and never received a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies and speculators are better off, because they kept unrestricted access to cheap leases on low- or no-potential federal land, and the government kept the existing leasing process.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas lessees and speculators

for.name: Rep. Susie Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through referral to the Natural Resources Committee.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees on June 19, 2021, and never scheduled a markup or committee vote; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; no vote ever occurred, so the party split was never tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Oil and gas lessees and speculators
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to acquire leases for the minimum bid, or noncompetitively, on federal land with little or no oil and gas potential — leases that rarely produce but can tie up the land and block other uses. Their business interest in cheap speculative leases runs directly against the taxpayer savings and public access the bill was meant to deliver.

industries.industry: Grazing, recreation, and other public-land users
industries.note: The bill's findings state that leases on no- or low-potential land limit other uses of the land, including grazing, recreation, and wildlife habitat. Ending speculative leasing would keep more of that land available for those uses.
